claims.text: High-pressure torsion can improve the hardness and strength of high-entropy alloys without sacrificing useful mechanical performance.
Room-temperature HPT at 5 GPa for 5 turns provides a controlled amount of lattice distortion.
HPT produces grain refinement in high-entropy alloys.
HPT introduces lattice distortions in high-entropy alloys.
Grain refinement and lattice distortion increase dislocation density and dislocation interactions.
Atomic-size-induced distortion or solid-solution effects can increase the strength and hardness of high-entropy alloys.
The increased dislocation density and interactions caused by HPT improve alloy strength and hardness.
Under the specified HPT conditions, Vickers hardness will increase by at least 20% relative to an untreated alloy of the same composition.
Under the specified HPT conditions, yield strength will increase by at least 15% relative to an untreated alloy of the same composition.
The predicted hardness and yield-strength improvements will occur without a significant reduction in ductility.
The hypothesis applies to face-centered-cubic high-entropy alloys containing at least five elements.
Conventional annealing provides a comparison condition that does not introduce significant lattice distortion.
The relevant HPT response can be evaluated by measuring Vickers hardness, yield strength, and elongation at break.
Failure to reach the specified hardness and strength improvements without substantial ductility loss would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The predicted outcome is defined relative to an untreated alloy of the same composition, but the experiment proposes conventionally annealed material as the comparison. Annealing is itself a treatment and may change grain size, defect density, phases, and mechanical properties, so it is not necessarily the stated untreated baseline.
